title: Flight 93 National Memorial, Stoystown, Pennsylvania
seoTitle: Charter Bus to the Flight 93 Memorial, Pennsylvania
excerpt: A charter bus to the Flight 93 National Memorial suits school and civic groups. What the site contains, how long to allow, and how to prepare a group.

heroImage.alt: The Wall of Names at the Flight 93 National Memorial standing along the flight path

extraImage.alt: The Tower of Voices, a ninety-three foot chime tower at the Flight 93 National Memorial

body.text: On 11 September 2001, forty passengers and crew aboard United Flight 93 forced their way toward the cockpit of a hijacked aircraft and brought it down in a Somerset County field rather than at its intended target in Washington. The memorial built on that field is quiet, deliberate and unusually affecting. A charter bus to the Flight 93 National Memorial is how most school and civic groups reach it, because the site sits well away from any town.

items: The Visitor Center Complex, with an exhibition covering the day itself, the passengers and crew, and the response. Allow an hour; it is the part groups underestimate.
The Memorial Plaza and the Wall of Names, forty inscribed marble panels standing along the flight path, at the edge of the impact site.
The boulder marking the impact point, visible from the plaza in a field that is otherwise left alone.
The Tower of Voices, a 93-foot tower holding forty wind chimes, each with a distinct tone. It stands near the park entrance and is worth stopping at on the way in rather than on the way out.

body.text: Admission is free — it is a National Park Service site. The walk from the Visitor Center down to the Memorial Plaza is a paved, gently sloping path of about a third of a mile, and there is separate parking at the plaza for anyone who cannot manage it.
Preparing a group, particularly a school group

This is a place where people died, and it is treated as such. Students born long after 2001 have no memory of the day and will take their cue entirely from how the visit is framed. A short briefing on the coach before arrival — what happened, why the site is quiet, what is expected — does more for the visit than anything the exhibition can do afterwards.
Rangers offer talks at the Memorial Plaza and can arrange programs for school groups if you contact the park in advance. It is free and it is substantially better than walking the site unguided.
Which charter bus suits the visit

items: Forty to fifty-six: a full-size [charter bus](/fleet/motor-coaches) is the standard vehicle, and there is designated bus parking at both the Visitor Center and the plaza.
Twenty to thirty-two: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) suits a smaller class, a historical society or a veterans' group.
Twenty-eight to sixty: a [school bus](/fleet/school-buses) works for districts within about two hours.

body.text: Our [school trip transportation](/services/school-trips) quotes carry the insurance documentation districts require, and we handle a steady volume of civic and veterans' group travel to this site each year.
Getting there and how long to allow

The memorial is near Stoystown in rural Somerset County, roughly ninety minutes east of Pittsburgh and about two and a half hours west of Harrisburg. We run pickups from [Somerset](/locations/pennsylvania/somerset), [Johnstown](/locations/pennsylvania/johnstown), [Pittsburgh](/locations/pennsylvania/pittsburgh) and [Altoona](/locations/pennsylvania/altoona).

Allow two and a half to three hours on site. Groups searching for charter bus rental near me for a memorial visit frequently budget an hour and then find themselves rushing the exhibition, which is the part of the visit that does the explaining. There is very little nearby in the way of food, so plan lunch either before you arrive or on the road afterwards.
Pairing it with other sites in the region

Somerset County is rural and the memorial is a half-day, so most groups build something around it. The obvious pairing for a school or architecture group is Fallingwater, Frank Lloyd Wright's house over a waterfall, about an hour southwest — tours are timed and must be booked well in advance, and group sizes are capped.

For a civic or veterans' group, the Johnstown Flood National Memorial and the Johnstown Flood Museum sit around forty minutes north and make a coherent day about disaster, response and memory. The Quecreek Mine Rescue Site is closer still, a few minutes from the Flight 93 entrance.

Whatever you add, keep the memorial first in the day rather than last. It is the stop people are quiet after, and following it with a gift shop or a lunch stop tends to land badly. Groups who visit in the morning and travel home in the afternoon consistently report the better trip.

The grounds are open year-round and the site is exposed — this is a high, open field, and it is cold and windy from November through March. May through October is far more comfortable, and September is the most meaningful time to visit but also the busiest around the anniversary. Check Visitor Center hours before you set the schedule, as they are shorter than the grounds' hours.

Contact the park first if you want a ranger program, then send us that time along with your headcount and pickup point. [Request an all-in quote](/quote) and you will usually have an itemized price back the same day, driver, fuel, tolls and taxes included.
